Long-term use of glucocorticoids comes with many serious and sometimes irreversible adverse effects, yet clinicians tend to maintain them in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients in remission for fear of triggering flares. This small observational study compared flare rates among propensity-matched SLE patients in clinical remission who had steroids tapered versus those staying on low-dose maintenance.
With 480 patients followed for a mean of 7 years, flare rates did not differ significantly between the groups, although patients with certain characteristics did show greater flare risk after stopping steroids. For patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in remission, flare risk was not increased after stopping all glucocorticoids in a small Italian study.
These results are potentially important insofar as they can inform clinical decision-making on whether patients with SLE in remission should try having steroids withdrawn. Long-term use, of course, comes with a raft of adverse effects that would be best to avoid. But clinicians have had to balance that with the risks from SLE flares, which can lead to irreversible organ damage along with the pain and discomfort associated with active lupus. Zen and colleagues cited several previous studies that also found no increase in flare risk with steroid discontinuation, but a 124-patient randomized trial published in 2020opens in a new tab or window found a fivefold increase in flares with discontinuation.
Theirs isn't exactly that study -- it was not randomized but rather compared patients whose clinicians decided on their own judgment whether to withdraw steroids for SLE patients in remission. Propensity matching certainly helps make the comparison meaningful, but the observational design remains an important limitation. Patients in the study were members of the prospectively assembled Padua Lupus Cohort, which had enrolled 541 SLE patients as of 2023.

ceramic.snippet: Study Guide   📖 Core Concepts Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) – a multisystem autoimmune disease where auto‑antibodies attack healthy tissues, causing flares and remission. Autoantibodies – most important are antinuclear antibodies (ANA) (high sensitivity) and anti‑double‑stranded DNA (anti‑dsDNA) (high specificity). Immune‑complex (type III) hypersensitivity – circulating immune complexes deposit in organs, activate complement, and drive inflammation. Complement consumption – low serum C3/C4 indicates active disease because complexes use up complement proteins. Classification vs. Diagnosis – ACR/1997 and 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria (≥4/11 items) are research tools; clinicians also rely on ANA, anti‑dsDNA, clinical picture. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) – cornerstone DMARD; reduces mortality (54 %), flares, and long‑term organ damage. Organ‑specific risk – kidney (lupus nephritis), heart (Libman‑Sacks endocarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis), CNS (neuropsychiatric SLE), skin (malar rash, discoid lesions). --- 📌 Must Remember Epidemiology: 9 × higher in women (child‑bearing age); prevalence 20–70/100 k. Key lab markers: ANA – sensitive (95 %) but not specific. Anti‑dsDNA – specific (70 % of pts); levels parallel disease activity. Low C3/C4 – sign of active immune‑complex disease. Antiphospholipid antibodies – ↑ thrombosis, false‑positive VDRL. ACR 1997 criteria: 4 of 11 items (malar rash, discoid rash, serositis, oral ulcers, arthritis, photosensitivity, hematologic disorder, renal disorder, ANA, immunologic disorder). First‑line medication: HCQ for all patients unless contraindicated. Steroid stewardship: Use lowest effective dose; chronic 5 mg pred equivalent ↑ CVD, osteoporosis, cataracts. Renal protocol: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) preferred for lupus nephritis; cyclophosphamide for severe/induction. Pregnancy safety: HCQ safe; avoid cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, high‑dose steroids when possible.

### Objective

Whether maintaining steroid-free remission is feasible in Indian patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

### Methods

In 148 patients with SLE including 78 lupus nephritis (LN) previously put into remission, steroid therapy was gradually tapered off.

# People in Lupus Remission Can Successfully Discontinue Prednisone When Withdrawal is Gradual
Although abrupt withdrawal from corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) has been associated with increased risk of lupus flares, new research finds that people with prolonged lupus remission can successfully stop taking the medication when it is discontinued gradually.
In fact, slowly phasing out the medication was not only safe in people with inactive lupus but was also associated with fewer flares and less damage accrual compared to maintaining a low prednisone dose.
The study included a total of 204 people with lupus in clinical remission for two years in a row.
Half (102) maintained a low and steady prednisone dose over two years (5 mg of prednisone per day), while the other half slowly reduced their dosage over many months and eventually stopped taking the drug entirely.
By the end of the first year, people in the prednisone withdrawal group had fewer flares than those in the maintenance group.
After two years, those who had discontinued the medication continued to have fewer flares, including fewer moderate to severe flares.
They also had less frequent damage accrual compared to those maintaining a low dose of prednisone.

The latest findings are very encouraging, suggesting that it is possible to gradually stop taking prednisone and maintain clinical remission in lupus.

### Objectives

To assess flare risk during remission in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients comparing low-dose glucocorticoid (GC) maintenance and its discontinuation.
